header.author: Victorinus Afrus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp119.tmp119.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.

Line 1: the lemma has 'contemptionem', evidently for 'contentionem' (contention), which the text uses later; translated so. 'Ut' before 'nobis incutiant' is printed 'at'. 'eruoe' read as 'cruce', 'indefensione' as 'in defensione'. The sentence 'invidiam enim dixit quod sentiant cum aemuli nobis sint' is compressed and the rendering is uncertain. Line 3: 'Pene andaciter' read as 'paene audaciter'; the sentence has no main verb, and '[It might seem]' is supplied. Line 4: 'Sequebatur Uti non continuo...' is awkward and may be corrupt; the rendering is tentative. Line 5: 'sive cum vitae mihi in poena erit' seems corrupt (perhaps 'cum vita mihi in poena erit'), and is translated in that sense. The passage that follows, on 'life with punishment', is also obscure.

In the Vers. 23 lemma 'quarto magis' is read as 'quanto magis'; 'vicere' (Vers. 22) as 'vivere'; 'in divisa' perhaps 'in diversa'. In Vers. 23 commentary 'etiam illam, lucrum consequi' is obscure, translated as 'that is, to obtain that gain'. In Vers. 28 'Hoc, inquit, non terreri Evangelio servientes' seems defective. 'Advocatio' (2:1) is rendered 'calling' following the commentator's interpretation. In 2:1 'dilectus et dilectionis' read as 'dilecti et dilectionis'; 'exere eatis' as 'exerceatis'. In Vers. 29 the lemma 'a Christo' presumably stands for 'pro Christo', as the commentary implies.

Line 15: 'recreatione' is uncertain (edition marks a note). Line 17: the sentence 'et quemadmodum non modo benignitate... revocavit' is evidently corrupt; translated literally. Line 16: 'unum scientes' read for the lemma's 'sentientes'; the commentator deliberately distinguishes them. 'ditectio', 'manis', 'putiorem', 'Hoc sapile' read as dilectio, inanis, potiorem, Hoc sapite.

Line 19: the end (‘id est caetera animalia (1) non quo hic (2)…’) is garbled in the edition; ‘[not of]’ is supplied by sense. Line 21: ‘>070?’ is read as λόγῳ; ‘logo’ as Logos. Line 20: ‘ύτπίχοος γςνόμινος’ read as ὑπήκοος γενόμενος; ‘subauditor’/‘obauditor’ rendered ‘obedient’. Line 22: the sentence about the error ‘among us’ is syntactically loose; rendering is tentative.

Line 23: 'etsi non sit' read as consequential ('so ... not'); sense requires that neither name is above the other. 'vita mors est' (also earlier) is obscure; possibly corrupt for 'vita mortem vicit' or similar. Line 24: 'in nobis praestans' taken as 'in our power'. Line 25: Greek 'τέχνα' read as τέκνα. 'faciendum enim vel non esse faciendam' read as 'whether it is to be done or not'.

Parenthesised numerals in the edition are footnote marks and are omitted. Evident scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'silaboro', 'Domitio' for Domino, 'scilis' for scitis, 'siculi' for sicuti, 'nisi eum' for misi eum, 'demo grotulemini' for denuo gratulemini); the verse heading 'Vers. 22, 20, 24' is taken as 22, 23, 24. Line 29: 'Scilicet quae secunda est pictas' is obscure; read as 'pietas' ('piety'), but the text may be corrupt. Line 31: 'alit enim ad alia loca' is corrupt; taken as 'alios enim ad alia loca [mittit]'. Line 33: 'Deinde quia et festinare ad mortem debemus' is translated as a question; the sense may require 'non' or 'nec' ('we ought not to hasten to death'). Line 33: 'omne quod ad vitam hic agimus ... et nobis protinus et aliis' lacks a verb; '[profits]' supplied.

35: 'niccum' read as 'mecum' ('towards me'). 36: 'non scribere' in the paraphrase contradicts the lemma and is translated as 'to write'; 'Graecus sit' read as 'sic'; the Greek is ἀσφαλές ('safe'). The psalm reference is to Ps. 67/68:24, where in the Latin the dogs' tongues are dipped in enemies' blood; 'saliari' is perhaps for 'satiari' ('sated'). 37: 'propter eminentiam carnis ejus' ('of his flesh') is odd and may be corrupt, perhaps for 'cognitionis' ('knowledge'). The claim about salvation and the circumcision of Moses is obscure; perhaps Exod. 4:24–26 is meant. 38: 'fywpat' is a garbled Greek word, read as ἡγοῦμαι ('I count'). 'In ilia' is read as 'in illo' ('in him'). 'Ni lucri' is read as 'ut lucri' ('so that he may gain'). 39: 'quam praedixit' is translated as written, though it is perhaps corrupt.

Several scanning errors read as evident: 'sum' for 'eum' (40), 'firmus' for 'fiamus' (40), 'rita' for 'vita' and 'consummator' for 'consummatur' (41), 'super(??)' for 'supernae' (42), 'doce' for 'duce' (42). In 42 'insectator legis' is odd (perhaps for 'sectator', 'zealot'); rendered 'zealot of the law'. In 43 the argument about the concessive versus suspended reading is compressed and partly obscure ('si autem non est istud, concedentes'; 'quod supra est non admittimus'); rendered literally. 'obvius fiam' rendered 'come to meet [him]'.

Victorinus's lemma has 'transfiguravit' (perfect, 'transfigured') where the Greek and Vulgate have a future; translated as given. In line 45, 'si aliter vixerim' ('if I live otherwise') is read as 'vixerint' ('if they live otherwise'), which the context requires. The heading 'Vers. 19' covers words from 3:18 to 3:19. In line 49, 'sit obscurum' is read as 'fit obscurum' ('it is obscure'). In the same line, 'quo referamus illi' means 'to what we should refer [the word] illi (to him)'; the English keeps 'to him' as a quoted word, which reads awkwardly. The sentence beginning 'Duo conclusit' in line 44 is compressed and its construction is uncertain.

51: 'germane unijuge' renders Greek γνήσιε σύζυγε; Victorinus takes it as Epaphroditus. 54: several readings are corrupt: 'cum orali me' read as 'cum oratione' (with speech); 'mundabis' read as 'mundanis'; 'impicantur' read as 'impleantur' (be fulfilled); 'Cujus autem non est honesta?' is obscure and probably corrupt, translated literally; 'bona gratia' (εὐχαριστία) rendered 'good thanks'. 55: 'habet omnem intellectum' follows Victorinus's text ('holds', not 'surpasses'). 56: Victorinus's comment treats 'vera, casta' (true, chaste) though the lemma as printed reads 'justa, sancta'; his text of the verse evidently included 'true' and 'chaste'. 'unde dixit ibi' is awkward and may be corrupt. 'fructura' read as 'fructum'.

Line 57: 'aduimliatur' read as 'adnuntiatur'; 'quae fuerat una' is obscure, perhaps corrupt (possibly 'quae fuerat varia' or similar); rendered loosely as '[at odds]'. Line 58: 'Novi sensus' read as 'Novi sensus [is]'; 'oratio cicura' read as 'oratio, cura'. Line 61: 'ut est communicatio, pari modo jungi mysterio' is obscure; translated literally. Line 65: 'ordo mihi suavitatis' read as 'odor mihi suavitatis'; 'ropletus' as 'repletus'.

Line 66: 'Deo... nostro, scilicet Jesu Christo patri nostro' is odd as printed and may be corrupt; translated as it stands. 'ex petieritis' read as 'expetieritis'. Line 67: 'monilis' read as 'monitis'. Line 68: 'vel mundo ni salutetis' is evidently corrupt; rendered as 'vel mando ut salutetis' ('or bid you greet'). Line 69: the first sentence is grammatically broken; the bracketed words supply a probable sense.

nodes.text: THE SINGLE BOOK OF VICTORINUS ON PAUL'S LETTER TO THE PHILIPPIANS.

Chapter 1. — Verse 15. — He has set out either four causes or four [kinds of] persons who proclaim Christ. Of these, two, the first and the last, [proclaim] out of malice; the two in the middle out of a good mind and goodwill. We must say how the first and the last differ from each other, and how the second and the third [differ] from each other. The first is from malice, on account of envy and contention: for he called it envy because they feel [this] since they are our rivals. The last is also itself from evil, as [in] Verse 17: some proclaim Christ out of defiance. That is, in order to harm us. For though they openly deny Christ, they have pretended to proclaim [him], so that we, who think and believe them to be adversaries, may be grieved that the same things are proclaimed by them as we proclaim. For out of defiance, he says, not holily or purely, they proclaim Christ; but in order to strike us with affliction and groaning and pain, so that they may show that they rejoice in our punishments and chains; just as it was said to Christ himself when he was set on the cross, If you are the Son of God, free yourself, so it may also be said to Paul: May your God free you from your chains; that Christ is God, he is God; but you are still in punishments. In this way, then, this preaching of the malicious differs from the former one: that [former one is] not in order to add punishments to the apostle's chains, but in order that they themselves may aim at the glory of preaching, since they do this through envy, not through understanding and their own will. But the double cause, or double [kind of] person, on the side of good stands thus: that some proclaim Christ through goodwill, some out of love. These two causes on the side of good are opposed one each to those on the side of evil: for this one, which is the second, answers to the first. For if the first preach Christ because they envy and because they contend, on the other hand some of the good proclaim Christ through goodwill, truly holding this, not envying us, but because what they hold is good and they have goodwill towards the Gospel. And the third cause, which is on the side of the good, is contrary to the one which is last on the side of the evil. For if that last one on the side of the evil is such that some proclaim Christ out of defiance for our punishment and affliction, this one on the side of the good is contrary, because some proclaim out of love: that is, following me and dear to me, not mocking me: namely, he says, because I have been set for the defence of the Gospel. For they know that I am in the defence of the Gospel, and that for this reason I endure these punishments of mine for the Gospel; hence they too proclaim Christ out of love, either love for Christ or love for me, not mocking me like those who preach Christ out of defiance; not purely, but supposing that they stir up affliction for my chains.

Verse 18. — What then? Provided that in every way, whether under pretext or in truth, Christ is proclaimed. Since above he set out four persons or causes [through which] Christ is proclaimed, he declares and shows that he is not at all disturbed by the malicious because they preach Christ. For in vain do they suppose that they stir up affliction for my chains. For what [is it], or why am I disturbed? Or why am I thrown into affliction? For I rejoice and am glad that Christ is proclaimed in every way: whether while they, under some pretext of their own or some occasion of their own, either of harming or of envying, preach Christ — so long as they preach — or whether they proclaim [him] in truth. For the outcome pleases me very greatly, that they make proclamation about Christ; and they both name Christ and confess [him as] God, though with a different intent, and as the Son of God. For when this is celebrated, practised, done, Christ is thus proclaimed by all, and we arrive at what we want, that Christ be proclaimed. If this is so, they supposed in vain that I would be thrown into affliction. Then he adds as follows: And in this I rejoice, yes, and I will rejoice. And I rejoice, he says, even in this very thing, that Christ is proclaimed. For even those who proclaim Christ by way of harming, so as to harm me, do not deny [him]; nor do those who proclaim Christ through envy, for their own purposes, and covertly, and with malicious words — yet they confess Christ and proclaim Christ: in this, he says, I rejoice and will rejoice.

Verse 19. — For I know that this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ. [It might seem] almost bold and rash [of me] to have accepted gladly and accepted with joy that Christ was proclaimed in whatever way, even by the wicked, even out of defiance, even through envy: but I affirm that this will be so out of trust in God and [his] goodwill, and, as he himself says, out of the supply of Christ and his Spirit; and I know it will be so, because this, in whatever way it is proclaimed, will be true, and will also be as that Paul himself wishes, who truly proclaims; and for this reason he says, For I know that this will turn out for my salvation: so that this which they proclaim, even for my ruin — those who proclaim Christ out of defiance, or those who proclaim Christ through envy and contention — all of it, nevertheless, I know will turn out for my salvation, Christ, that is, and his Spirit supplying [it]: according, he says, to what I expect, and I have hope, so I have confidence that they will never harm me, even if they proclaim Christ for another reason, that I may suffer punishments and be tormented: yet since my hope and expectation are of Christ, this will turn out for my salvation.

Verse 20. — That in nothing shall I be ashamed; but with all confidence, as always, so now also Christ will be magnified in my body. It followed that this very thing which the malicious preach, which they preach through envy, which they preach out of defiance, might not straightway turn out for salvation, [but] might bring him both ruin and punishments, so that he would be ever in chains, and indeed even in death — but [he says] either way. For the apostle, looking ahead, says that it will come about that Christ is preached whatever the outcome: for never, he says, shall I be ashamed, but from either I shall be glad with joy and rejoice, and as always, so now too, he says, Christ will be magnified: in my body, he says; that is, when my body, subjected to every punishment, endures everything, and preaches Christ, and does not cease, and is not terrified by punishments, and does not yield to all punishments. What he means by all punishments he himself explains by adding whether through life or through death. For whether I live enduring punishments, Christ will be preached; or whether I die under punishments, he will be preached more and more; when all see that I was neither deterred by punishments nor called back by death, but in the Gospel either spent my life with punishments or endured punishments even to death, and yet persevered in preaching the Gospel.

Verse 21. — For to me to live is Christ and to die is gain. So I do not fear death, because to die is gain for me: not death itself [is] gain, but dying; and life is Christ, because whoever hopes in him lives always, both now and hereafter. For when he said, Christ will be magnified in my body, whether through life or through death, referring to this life: if he overcomes those who lay snares for him, and perseveres in the Gospel, his life will be glorious, because it glories in Christ, not in chains, not in safety, not in suffering nothing. But if he is killed, to die is gain, since for him life is Christ. Thus he has given each its own answer; so that to death he answered, I do not fear death, since for me life is Christ: whether in life, or in chains though they bind me, still for me life is Christ, and to die itself is gain, since I come to Christ. Or both of these are assigned to each of the preceding [terms]: I do not fear death, because life for me is Christ and to die is gain; or when my life will be in punishment, I do not fear life, because life for me is Christ. Therefore they achieve nothing, whether they hand me over to death or give me up to torments in life: for neither harms me, because for me in torments life is not life with punishment, since life for me is Christ; or if they kill [me], this too is no punishment for me, because life for me is Christ, and to die is gain.

Verse 22. — But if [I] live in the flesh, this is for me the fruit of [my] work. Since he said above, for me life is Christ, and it was uncertain which life he meant, whether this one which is in the flesh or that one which comes afterwards, he added [a word] about this life, which is here in the flesh, and said that nonetheless even in this life, while we live here in the flesh, there is for me, he says, the fruit of work. What is this fruit of work? That by my labour and by the Gospel I proclaim Christ, and bring about for many the hope of life and salvation, when they have begun to hope in Christ and to give faith to the Gospel. This, he says, is for me the fruit of work, even living in the flesh. And what I shall choose I do not know. For whether I die — because death is gain, and for me life is Christ, and I certainly come to him when I die here in the flesh — or again whether I live here in the flesh — because for me the fruit of work is to proclaim Christ and to preach the Gospel — what I shall choose, he says, I do not know: whether I should seek death, or still remain in life.

Verses 23, 24. — But I am hard pressed between the two, having the desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, which is much better by far. But that I remain in the flesh [is] necessary for your sake. A double necessity and desire, he says, draws me in divided directions; for I both have the desire to be dissolved, that is, to depart from the body, and to be with Christ — that is, to obtain that gain — which is indeed best and to be chosen. But again there is for me a necessity that I remain in the flesh and persevere for your sake. Thus to the first part he assigned desire, to wish to be dissolved and to be with Christ, because it is the highest and foremost and best; but here, that he should still remain in the flesh, he called a necessity rather than that [desire]: that I should live for this, to instruct you, to strengthen you in the Gospel. Since, then, he has as it were two desires, he confirms one, that he will still remain here in the flesh; and this I know with confidence, that I shall remain, and continue with you, for your progress and the grace of faith. Truly as a father, truly as a servant of God, of his two desires he as it were abandons that one which would have benefited himself alone, namely to depart at once, to be dissolved at once and to be with Christ.

Verse 25. — I am confident, he says, and I know with confidence that God will make me still be here, so that I remain; and I shall continue, so as to benefit you all, and that you may have progress to the glory of faith. I shall remain, he says, and he added more, and I shall continue, that is, I shall remain until completion; and [he means] the completion of your progress, that you may advance and obtain grace, namely [the grace] of faith; that is, that by showing faith you may earn grace from God.

Verse 26. — That your glory and exultation may abound in Christ Jesus in me, through my presence with you again. That is, when I have begun to be with you again — this is through my presence with you again — your glory may exult, and the exultation itself may abound in Christ Jesus in me, through my presence with you again: that is, that I, being present, may perceive how your glory exults and abounds in Christ, in that you love Christ, in that you serve Christ, in that you rejoice to serve Christ.

Verse 27. — Only conduct yourselves worthily in the Gospel of Christ. The whole sum of the Christian life is this: to conduct oneself in the Gospel of Christ, to proclaim him to oneself and to others, to have hope in him, to do everything one does according to his commandments: this is to conduct oneself worthily in the Gospel of Christ. But even this is too little; therefore it must be added that we conduct ourselves in the Gospel of Christ before all things, and conduct ourselves worthily. To conduct oneself worthily is to live according to his precepts and to do those things which Christ commands. So that whether I come and see you, or in absence I hear of you, that you stand in one spirit, striving with one soul together with the faith of the Gospel. He himself explains what it is to conduct oneself worthily in the Gospel of Christ: standing in one spirit, striving with one soul together with the faith of the Gospel. Standing, he says, in one spirit: because the spirit is one when we now have understanding, and perceive the Gospel, and live accordingly. But this is the work of the soul, that we drive out the adversities of the body: therefore [he says] striving with one [soul] together with the faith — the faith which the Gospel has given you. Therefore stand, he says, in one spirit, and wrestle together with one soul with the faith of the Gospel.

But this explanation contains what he said above, conduct yourselves worthily in the Gospel of Christ. And how the words hang together so as to be complete and connected, we shall consider thus: conduct yourselves, he says, worthily in the Gospel, so that I may hear of you worthily that you stand in one spirit and strive with one soul together with the faith of the Gospel. And I may hear even in absence; but there will be confirmation, so that what I hear I may believe when I come to you and see you. Whether I hear of you in absence, then in both ways I shall see you, that you stand in one spirit.

Verse 28. — And that you are not terrified in anything by your adversaries: and this work too belongs to the explanation of what it is to conduct oneself worthily in the Gospel of Christ — never to be terrified by adversaries, nor to be terrified in anything: since to them it is a demonstration of destruction, but to us of salvation. This, he says, [is] not to be terrified, [for those] serving the Gospel. That is, every act of a Christian is for salvation: not to be thrown into confusion by adversities, to believe the faith of the Gospel in Christ, to suffer for Christ, and at the same time also to know that [this] comes from the grace of God. Therefore this thing, he says, not to be terrified in anything by adversaries, is both for our salvation and for our adversaries a cause of destruction: and yet this is the gift of God. And this from God: lest we think it is our own work that not being terrified is a cause of salvation for us; for this too is from God, as I have often warned, so that all things come about by God's will and mercy and grace.

Verses 29, 30. — For it has been granted to you by Christ. He joins these precepts to the whole exhortation: for it belongs [here] to show what it is to conduct oneself worthily in the Gospel of Christ, according to the precepts above; and now an exhortation is added that they believe in Christ; and not only believe, but also suffer for him. And what they are to suffer he adds: either what you have seen in me, or what you have heard of me: for this is to conduct oneself worthily in the Gospel of Christ, and this has been given us as a gift on behalf of Christ, because he fulfilled the mystery and suffered all things for our liberation. On his account, then, he gave us the gift that we believe in him. And a great gift it is, if by faith in him alone we earn such grace. But let us so believe that we also suffer for him; for he adds this: Having the same struggle and contest which you both saw in me and have heard of me. That you too, believing in Christ, may suffer all things for him, that is, on his account. For to do all things, and not to turn to another, and to suffer all things for him — this is the struggle: and this contest we have, namely both the striving and the straining, which leads to the palm and the crown. So that you may not be ignorant of this contest, it is the one you saw in me — namely concerning the chains, the prison, all the evils which Paul endured: both of which give you certainty that I suffered, since you have either heard or seen.

Chapter 2. — Verses 1, 2, 3, 4. — If then there is any calling in Christ, if any consolation of love, if any fellowship of the spirit, if any heart and compassion, fulfil my joy, that you all think the same. Being about to ask a favour, that his joy may be fulfilled — which joy is committed to this precept, that you all think the same, that no one disagree (for then there is both charity and concord, when all think the same; and if there is concord, the apostle will have this joy) — so, in order to obtain what he wishes to be his joy, through their unanimity, concord and same mind, and other such things, he first sets out as it were an account of merits, what he deserves from them, that his joy may be fulfilled in this, that all think the same, and the rest. And these are the grounds of merit: that they have been called together in Christ; for God calls us in Christ; for he sanctifies those whom he has called and chosen and whom he has ordained. The calling, then, is first: if, he says, there is any calling in Christ among us, in that we have been called together, and called in Christ, and [there is] my merit towards you, then fulfil my joy. This, then, is the first ground of merit among them, that they should listen to one another: that they have been called in Christ. And from the fact that they have been called in Christ there is also love. Next he adds if any consolation of love. For when we are in evils and labour under the evils of the world, if we love one another, God will be to us the consolation of love. If then, he says, this is the consolation of love — that because I love you, you should console me in the evils in which I am — then fulfil my joy. So this must be added to each [clause]. Then he added, if any fellowship of the spirit. In good order this is third: for first is to be called in Christ, next to have love; and when both are present — that I am now called in Christ, and they have among themselves the consolation of the beloved and of love — without doubt there is fellowship of the spirit. If, he says, there is any fellowship of the spirit. Let us hear [again] that fulfil my joy. Then he adds, if any heart and compassion. For one body of the Church is formed when those called in Christ are joined to one another in charity; they are joined also in spirit, and become one heart and one compassion. If then any heart — if there is a heart of compassion — [it serves] to this end, that there be the calling in Christ and the fellowship in the spirit. And compassion serves to this, if there is any consolation of love, that each console the other, since we are always in evils in the world: since we are the same heart, we ought to show compassion to one another. So then, if any heart of compassion, fulfil my joy. And what joy, he added: that you think the same, all the very same thing. What is that you think the same? He sets it out through what follows, either in what they should think the same, or how they should think the same: — Exercise the same love, being of one soul, thinking one thing, [doing] nothing through contention or through empty glory, but in humility of mind each considering yourselves surpassed by others. Let each of you look not only to his own things, but each to those of others.

Verse 5. — For think this in yourselves which [was] also in Jesus Christ. As I said, this is the exhortation which he is now carrying out with fuller precepts: fulfil, he says, my joy, [and he shows] in what things it can be brought about. These precepts, as he has always taught, contain what is to be done and also what is not to be done. What is to be done he adds thus: that you all think the same, that you all exercise the same love, of one soul, thinking one thing. He inserts what is not to be done: nothing through contention or through empty glory. And again he adds what is to be done: but through humility of mind each considering yourselves surpassed by others. Again he adds what is not to be done: let each not look to his own things. Then what is to be done: but each to those of others. Then he adds this, which is of the greatest weight for exhortation, and a sure exhortation drawn from the precepts, in which the conclusion of the precept is this: that each should think about the refreshment of others. This, he says, you ought to do and establish and think in yourselves, which Christ did: that, thinking of others, he thought nothing of himself and of his own glory; or of the fact that, as he will teach, he himself laid down his power in order to come to the aid of all others. So this is held in the exhortation, that the joy of Paul himself may be fulfilled.

Let us see, then, what the precepts are one by one. First he says that [you think] the same: the power, the right and the working of all Christianity is this, not to disagree, but to hold one and the same thing in mind. For if there is one God, if there is one Son of his, if there is one Holy Spirit, if all these three are one, so we too ought to hold as one what we think, so that we all think the same. Then follows that we exercise the same love. This now belongs to moral discipline, that is, to life; the former to knowledge. For since I have said that there are two kinds [of teaching] in Paul, and in every treatise — that some things are learned for knowledge, others are learned for acts and for life — so here too [there is] for knowledge what is set down as that you think the same; then for life, that you exercise the same love. What is the same? The same that another [shows] toward you, you [show] toward the other; and not a divided love, but love in Christ. That is the same love. Then he added: of one soul, knowing one thing. He seems to me to have repeated in reversed order the same things that were said above. For of one soul is one [thing], which relates to the same love; another is knowing one thing, which [relates to], as I said above, that you all think one thing. But there is also something more in these two than in the earlier ones. For it is one thing to say that you all think the same, another knowing one thing, though in the same [matter], since both belong to knowledge. But that earlier thinking the same means that, while knowledge is not yet confirmed, the capacity for knowing nevertheless appears equal — not yet completed — [while the latter is] knowledge already perfected. In the second precept, then, though both are in one sense, it is nevertheless put more strongly: knowing, he says, one thing: this is now the precept itself, when he said knowing. But above he said thinking the same, that is, having the same perceptions of understanding: so that is still in act, this can be seen in perfection. Thinking the same, and likewise with regard to life, is also in act: concerning life, that you exercise the same love. Moreover, of one soul is in perfection, and both concern conduct and the manner of life: hence, though the individual items seem the same each to each, the later ones are the stronger. Then he added: nothing through contention or through empty glory. For there could still be contention, both in thinking the same and in knowing the same. So the manner that ought to be — or rather that ought not to be — is given in what is added: nothing, he says, through contention. For many have either a need or a wish to contend. So he removed both kinds of contention, so that there be neither need nor wish to contend, since both are faulty. Some rush into contention out of curiosity; others are by nature such as to be contentious: therefore it was added, nothing through contention. Then again, others put this forward for boasting, so that they contend and appear equal, or stronger through stubbornness in resisting, and superior or [able] to boast. This, then, he wants removed, and he says, nor through empty glory. For empty glory is wanting to please by speeches, to please by great cleverness and by contentiousness in argument. For with a Christian there ought rarely to be contention, and no boasting in speech.

To this later precept, thus set down, that we not appear to do anything through empty glory, there is necessarily added: but through humility of mind. For thus empty glory can be removed, if there is humility in the minds, that is, in the understandings; for he set down these as minds. By way of inquiry, let [each] put forward whatever he treats, not by assuming authority. Each considering yourselves surpassed by others. For truly this is humility, if you think every other person better: for this is to consider yourselves surpassed by one another; so that no one should think of another otherwise than to esteem him better, and as surpassing and being superior. If it is so, this is humility of mind. Then he adds: Let each of you look not to his own things, but to those of others. From this sense is linked what is added afterwards. Meanwhile this is to be referred to what came before: for then you will fulfil my joy, if you also do this, that each looks not only to his own things but to those of others, and so each have concern for others and for others' cares. For this is what we suppose: that if we think only of ourselves, we can benefit ourselves, and deal only with our own affairs, with our hope, with our liberation: but this is too little. For then we truly deal with ourselves if we also care for others and hasten to benefit others. For since we are all one body, if we provide for others we provide for ourselves; if we think of others, we think the more of ourselves. Hence he adds how great is this thing he urges, how outstanding, how forceful, when he says: Let us have this same thing in our minds which [was] also in Christ Jesus. What this is — Think this in yourselves which you think in Christ Jesus — he himself sets out and explains. For if we think this in Christ Jesus, that he took care rather for others, that is, for us, not for himself, nor for what he himself could or was able or is able [to do], but rather thought of us — this is what he said above: but let each of us take care for those of others. For our Lord Christ the Saviour, being indeed the Saviour, brought salvation to others: and how not only using kindness, nor shining with his goodwill does he clothe and cover [us] with his light, nor did he call [us] back to himself by kindness poured out and by majesty. So that we might know his kindness as greater and the greatest, he emptied himself, he says, and stripped himself of all majesty, so that, descending into flesh and taking on all that endurance of humility, in order to benefit us in the flesh, he bore injuries in the flesh, then the cross and death. All of which teach and exhort us, likewise imitating the Lord, to think of others rather than of ourselves. For this is truly to deal with ourselves: to take up the care of others for their salvation. This, then, is that you think this in yourselves which you also think in Christ: you perceive that he benefited others; therefore think this also in yourselves, that you take thought for others and take up concern for others, so that you may be able to benefit others.

Verses 6, 7, 8. — Who, though he was established in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal to God; but also emptied himself and took the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in bearing as a man. He humbled himself, made subject even to death, and the death of the cross. Two things, that is, two precepts, he had given above: one, that they should love humility; the other, that they should care not only for their own things but also for those of others. And he says: Mind this in yourselves which [was] also in Christ Jesus. What, then, of these two do we take in Christ Jesus? One? And which one? Or rather both? For one, concerning humility, is plain: that Christ humbled himself and took the person of a servant. Yet the second precept can also be here: for he endured thus for the sake of others, and thought of others rather than of himself. Here is briefly set out what Christ is, even before he descended into flesh, and in what power and substance he is. For it is said that Christ was the form of God. But what is the form of God? Not a shape, not a face, but image and power. I have touched on this fully here [in the commentary] on Ephesians, and treated it more fully and abundantly in other books: that God is in that which is the primal being itself; and being itself is primally to have, to live and to understand. But to understand and to live is a certain form and image of existence itself. Since, then, God is existence, as is proved by many [arguments], and rather that which is above existence; and the form of existence is to be moved, to understand, to live — for that being, which is invisible and incomprehensible, is in a way given form round about and defined, that is, called into consideration and knowledge, as to what it is, [when] it is understood as living and understanding. Thus being is the Father, while living and understanding, which are these very things in that which is being, [are] as it were [its] form. Christ, then, is the form of God: for Christ is life, and knowledge and understanding. This, then, is the form and image of God. How great the power, how great the deity or virtue, has been expressed elsewhere. So now Paul says: Christ did not, he says, consider it robbery — that is, he did not claim this for himself, wish only to have it, that he was the form of God; but he also emptied himself of power, so as to descend to the world and to the flesh, and take the form of man, that is, the image of one small and lowly.

But I think this must be attended to carefully and keenly: that although he himself says that he was sent by God, and that he fulfils the will of the Father, this mystery is so set down that it is of his own will that he came, and that he took the form or image of a servant. For thus he says: who, though he was established in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal to God; but emptied himself, and took the form of a servant. But since we always join [them] thus, and grasp this by necessity of understanding, that in that which is being there are understanding and life — so that even in God, who has this power, that he is being and supplies being to all, there is nevertheless that understanding, as living, or above understanding and above life and above existence — Christ, who is life, a life that has also gone forth from God, is in [him], and in that the very life is existence and the very understanding, he is equal to God: whence also the Father is in the Son, and the Son is in the Father. But these things, as I said, [are treated] more fully elsewhere. Therefore, when the Father willed, the Son willed; and when the Son willed, the Father willed. Hence both are rightly [said]: both that he was sent by the Father, and what is set down here, that he emptied himself. But let us understand that he emptied himself, not in this sense, that he laid aside his power somewhere or deprived himself [of it], but that he humbled himself to every base thing, descending to the lowest offices. When he fulfilled these, he emptied himself and his power. For taking flesh and the form and likeness of man, he suffered, did and fulfilled all things that belonged to man. For this is what he says: made in the likeness of man, and found in bearing as a man. For those are not to be listened to who say that he was a phantom, because it is said here, in the likeness of man; rather it refers to God, and to the Logos itself formed through the taking up of flesh in the likeness of men. For since flesh on earth has various forms, and it is manifest that Christ received flesh, it was said in what likeness, in the likeness of men, that is, [not of] the other animals, not that here [only] a likeness of men was in Christ, [and] not the man himself taken up.

Then it was added, after likeness, also bearing, so that he bore himself as a man. Thus he added, found as a man. The Greek indeed said σχῆμα; the Latin named it bearing. So since two things are set down in the Greek, in likeness and bearing, let us take bearing as figure, and how a man bears himself. For every quality of a man is expressed by these two, likeness and figure. For a likeness of man could be of immense size, as in giants, as in faces and limbs that are fashioned [by artists]; therefore he added: and the figure of man, so that a definite bearing and measure, besides the likeness of man, might be seen to have been taken up. Further, when he said found as a man, this was not said here with doubt, as a man, as if he had not been a man but a phantasm of a man; but it was said, found as a man, that is, with this middle way of speaking, by which he was truly not [merely] a man but God, and, having received flesh and figure, as a man. And as for his saying, he took the form of a servant: since he himself was the form of God, and man is the servant of God, therefore it was said, he took the form of a servant. By this he humbled himself and emptied himself, made, he says, subject unto death, that is, of the cross. See, in this very [phrase], when he said, made subject — but in Greek openly and fully, since it is said ὑπήκοος γενόμενος, that is, made obedient — in this very thing, as he said, is expressed what we said a little before, that he was sent by the Father. For if [he was] obedient, that is true and soundly said, who sent me here, and made subject; certainly both can be taken and understood not only by that reasoning, that God is also in Christ, and the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, but because we also find something similar in many places, that the authority belongs to the one sending, and the will to the one obeying. For as among the poets, when the father, sending Mercury, sent him by his command, Mercury, while obeying the father’s command, readied himself, and emptied himself so as to fly and pursue his journey — if it is right to compare such things with divine things — it may be understood both that Christ was sent by the command of the Father, God almighty, and that Christ the Son, by the very fact that he obeyed the command, emptied himself, so as to take the form of man, and come in flesh, and bear the image of a servant, humbling himself and made obedient, and obedient unto death. Which death? For there are many kinds of death: for first, to be in the flesh is [a kind] of death; then to take on all the sins of the flesh is itself death: therefore it was added, unto death. Which death? Of the cross, he says. For the Saviour did not free us by death, but freed us by the death of the cross: for the whole mystery [lies] not in death alone, but [in the death] of Christ, and indeed in the death of the cross: whence Paul said that he had faith in Christ, and in Christ himself crucified.

Verses 9, 10, 11. — What is gathered from all these? That Christ both took thought for others and made himself lowly. Wherefore God also exalted him, and gave him a name, that at the name of Jesus all should bend the knee, of those in heaven, on earth, and below the earth; and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father. What this is that has now been said — that God therefore exalted his Son and gave him the name which is above all names — and what this very name is, and why he has now given and granted these things, although it is [a matter] of great treatment and great learning, nevertheless we briefly point out what sort of thing it is. Christ, that is the Logos, who is with God, and at God’s side, next to God, and therefore is himself also God — to which Logos it came about from his working that he was both Christ [and] Jesus, and was exalted, and received a name above all names — this Logos, I say, in that he is Logos, is the form of God, is truly joined, coupled, and is one [with him], and therefore the Logos also is God, through whom all things were created, and in whom what was made is life, and this was from the beginning, and without the Logos nothing was made — he who is joined. Let ears take this simply: was he not called Son at that very time? It can indeed be understood that, since by the power of God, as God himself, and the form of God, himself God, he received this name and this title afterwards, after descending into the world, that is, into matter (ὕλη), he cut off matter itself, and conquered, and overcame death, so that death no longer had dominion. And if these works of his were so great, and the mercy of God so great, [and] through this the task was fulfilled by him, on his return and going back he received this name, and from this he was exalted, and obtained this grace, that he received the name of Son, which name is above every name.

But catholic teaching says that there was always the Father and always the Son: and so it must both be said and understood. Nevertheless, since among us this error has arisen, that it is held that before the descent into flesh the Logos was never called Son, this exposition does not now run that way either, though it holds its own view: that since it is said that he emptied himself, and though he was the form of God, he received the form and figure of a servant, found and made in the likeness of man, and humbled himself unto death, even the death of the cross, and since it is then added, wherefore God exalted him: he seems to have been exalted because of the passion itself, and to have received this grace, to receive this name which is above every name, for this cause, I say. For so Paul says. And if this is so, he wants it understood, as it were, that the name did not exist before this, though he was the power of God, was the Logos, was also the form in that he was Logos, and God, and was with God: and therefore it is as though it were not fitting that he received the name of son then, but after he was sent. In this we understand now that, from the fact that he was sent, that one is Father and this one Son: then, because of the works, because of the mystery, because of the passion, by which life [is] death, by the very death of Christ — because of this grace, I say, he received the name which is above every name; so that only the name was added, the reality was the same: also before, that is, the Logos and the power itself; not that the reality first existed now, when he came into flesh. But when the reality came, that is, power, and wisdom, and act, and operation, he was nevertheless called Logos, and was the Logos. But now the Logos himself, when he put on flesh, as was said — the Logos himself, I say, after the passion, and after the death of the cross, by which he conquered all death and all sins, received the title of Son, which title is above every name. For what is there that could be taken as equal, that could be compared with the name of Son? For friendship, kinship of blood, brotherhood and the rest are all inferior; whether [names] of ministers or of angels, or whatever others we might mention. The Son, therefore, is above every name: which name God gave to Christ after the passion, after the cross.

It may seem, however, that it is hardly so, that it should be true that the Son is above every name. For if one is not called son unless there is a father, and father unless there is a son, is this name, Son, then above that name which is Father? Certainly not. How, then, when the Son received a name, did he receive [one] above every name? Certainly [these words] are without doubt to be taken with regard to other names, and this name of Son is above all other names. For the Father is joined with the Son, and these names are equal, as far as names go; so the name Son is not above the name of Father, nor the name Father above the name of Son. That power which is called Father is above, above that power which is called Son; yet the names, whether Son or Father, are equal to one another. And if this is so, the Son is above every name, because the Father together with the Son is above every name; to which name, and in which name, of Jesus Christ, every man bends the knee and prays: and not man only, but all heavenly things and all earthly things, and all things under the earth which are said to be lower. And likewise, Verse 11: Every voice confesses that Jesus Christ our Lord is in the glory of the Father, and always was. This glory, therefore, was also given so that he himself is the glory of the Father, since the Father also begot him; and by him the world was created and saved, and life [is] death; and salvation and eternity, which was sought by all these. Those who believe in him have conquered death in the death of Christ.

Verses 12, 13: Therefore, my dearest, as you always obey, not as in [my] presence only, but much more now in [my] absence, work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you, both in will and in effect, according to [his] good will. After the mystery of the whole dispensation was set forth, which had been placed there so that the precept might be confirmed by which he warned that no one should think of himself, nor take care [only of himself], as our Lord Jesus also did in his mystery, there is added, as I said, an exhortation that they love one another: first when he called them dearest and most beloved to him; then, he says, just as you were obedient to me, so you always obey, not in [my] presence only, but more and more in [my] absence, and you have obeyed with fear and trembling. But why more and more? Either because days go forward, or because in absence the one who warns is to be feared more. And what is this, that he exhorts and warns them to act and work out their salvation, and to act observing and obeying, with fear, he says, and trembling? So that fear refers to the mind, and trembling to the body. It is a great mystery, which we ought to hear attentively, that by taking counsel and care for others we work out salvation more for ourselves. Then, that it is in our power to work out salvation for ourselves. For so he said, work out your salvation. But again, lest each one return too little thanks to God, if he should seem to work out salvation for himself, this was added: For it is God who works in you, both in will and in effect, according to [his] good will. Therefore work out your salvation, he says: but the working itself is nevertheless from God: for God works in you, and works so that you will thus. And the willing is as it were ours, whereby we work out salvation for ourselves. And yet, because the willing itself is worked in us by God, it comes about that we have both the working and the will from God. Thus both are mixed, so that we both have the will, and the will itself is God's; and because we have the will, effect is present according to [his] good will. And he binds man's fear more tightly when he says, For it is God who works in you. For if it is God who works in them, without doubt we ought to be in fear, lest we act against God's will, either by doing too little, or not with fear and trembling. And God works in us both to will and to act, according to [his] good will. So he who does not work from God first does not have the willing; then, even if he should have the willing, he does not have the effect, because he does not have good will.

Verses 14, 15: Do all things without murmurings and hesitations or reconsiderations. These are two warnings: that when we do something, now trusting, now believing in God, and carry out the divine commands, whether apostolic or prophetic or evangelical, we should not have murmuring, that is, complaints about obeying when we obey; and that, he says, we should do nothing either with some doubt or with reasoning and reconsideration [whether] it is to be done or not to be done. Or because, if you complain, you act from necessity, and that is not the good will of one who obeys. That you may be without complaint (the Greek says, that you may be without blame): that is, that there may be no complaint about you; and the Latin may have said this, without complaint and blameless. Then this follows: And sincere children of God, unblemished, in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation. For if you live in this way and obey in this way, you will not be blemished, says the Latin. The Greek, however, put it thus: τέκνα, that is, children without reproach. This is also what was said above: but be sincere now, where [you are] in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation. What does this mean? That a saved soul becomes a child of God in this way, if it lives so as it does now, while it is in the world, in the midst, in a crooked and perverse generation, that is, in this life. Therefore, while we are in this life, we must labour so that, fleeing this perversity and the crookedness of this generation, that is, of the creation in which we are, we may live unblemished, without reproach, sincere children of God, doing all things without reproach and without reconsideration. It is not enough, therefore, only to do, but to do in such a way that there is in us no reconsideration or murmuring and complaint about doing. And if we do these things in this life, the mind already devoted to God is then placed among the children of God, if it does God's precepts willingly, eagerly, without complaint; and does them now while it is in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation. Among whom you shine like lights in the world. A great exhortation, that already in this very state, in which we are in this world, we should stand out already in this crooked and perverse generation: and stand out so that we are lights of the world, which [are] in the world itself, like the sun and moon and the other shining stars. For by faith and knowledge of God, living according to the divine precepts, Christians excel, and exist as light and splendour in this world. For if, beyond other men, they conquer all things that are evil, and crush hidden demons, and expose iniquities, conquering darkness and the works of darkness, they act in this world as lights, and furnish light to all.

Verse 16: Holding fast the word of life, for my glory in the day of Christ. It is both a reward for you that you live thus, since you are lights in the world; and you will be for my glory in the day of Christ, that is, when Christ comes to judge. I have glory through you, because you hold fast the word of life, that is, because you have known Christ, who is the word of life: for in Christ what was made is life. Therefore Christ is the word of life. From this it is known how great is the benefit and how great the glory of those who correct the souls of others. For I have not run in vain. This will be my glory, he says, through the day of Christ, that I have freed you, and my labour has not laboured in vain nor run in vain. Labour is the genus; running is a species of labour. So when he had set out the genus, I have not laboured in vain, which could be by body or by tongue or by admonition or by persistence, he added a definite species, I have not run in vain. This is either the labour of the journey, or the labour of feeling, to persuade [them] of this, and to persuade quickly: this is, I have not run in vain.

Verses 17, 18. — But if I labour in the sacrifice and service of your faith, I am glad and I rejoice with you all. In the same way you too be glad with me. What was given above by way of precept is here set out as exhortation: that we should have care not only for ourselves, but that each should also have care for others. And if this is so, rejoicing too arises from us. He says this of us and of others. But if I labour, he says, in the sacrifice and service of your faith, that is, so that I am ready even to die for you, provided that I serve you and strengthen your faith, I am glad and I rejoice with you all. So then you too be glad with me, so that we all alike both bear care for ourselves and rejoice in one another.

Verse 19. — But I hope in the Lord Jesus Christ to send Timothy to you quickly, so that I too may be of good heart, knowing how things stand with you. This belongs to the instructions. And he truly bears care for them, since he promises to send another who will furnish the same things to them, and from whom he may learn what the Philippians are doing. He promises that he will shortly send his dearest Timothy. And since every act of ours must be assigned to God, so that it may be completed by God, I hope, he says, in the Lord Jesus Christ, that I will send Timothy to you, and send him quickly. The reason why he sends him is added: so that I too may be of good heart, knowing what you are doing, or how matters stand with you. As for his saying, so that I too may be of good heart: for I hope that you are of good heart, because you keep all the precepts and faith in Jesus Christ, whence you are of good heart; and for that reason I wish to send Timothy quickly, so that I too may be of good heart when I learn how things stand with you, whether from your conduct or from that of others.

Verses 20, 21. — For I have no one who is of one soul with me. He shows why he promises Timothy, and gives reasons: because he has no one of one soul, that is, who bears the same mind. You have one reason. He added another: who is faithfully concerned for you. Truly this is the man to be sent, who is both dearest to me and bears care for you and has concern on your behalf. For all seek their own things, not the things of Jesus Christ. Since he said that he is alone, and I have no one, he says, who is of one soul with me, what reasons does he give concerning the others? Namely, what the second is: piety. For if Timothy is given as one who is faithfully concerned for you, he added this reason too, a vice and a sin: all seek their own things, that is, they are anxious, they defend their own things, they guard their own things, and this is not [the mark] of a Christian. For what does it befit a Christian to seek in any companion and brother, rather than the things that are Christ's, that is, faith in Christ, fellowship, love, knowledge? Yet the things that are [Christ's] can also be understood as preaching the gospel of Christ.

Verses 22, 23, 24. — But you know his proof very well. That is, you have a testing of him: so the Greek put it. You ought to know; perceive and learn what proof of him I have. Accordingly what follows is rightly joined on: that as a son with a father he has served with me in the Gospel. It is therefore plain what is meant by they seek not the things of Jesus Christ. Timothy, he says, has served with me in the Gospel as a son with a father. He shows briefly how he served, although he had said he has served with me in the Gospel. But how did he serve? As a son serves a father: Timothy served with me in the Gospel in love and greater devotion; for he served with me, he says, not served me. Him therefore I hope to send soon. After he has commended his person and affection and diligence, he added that he will send such a man. I hope, he says, to send. This too [was said] above: I hope in the Lord. And his saying soon is the same as quickly above. As soon as I see how things stand with me, I will send Timothy; but when I see how things stand with me. And I trust in the Lord that I myself also will come shortly. With great affection and great admonition he added this, that although he is sending Timothy, he nevertheless promises that he himself will come.

Verse 25. — For I trust, he says, in the Lord that all will go well with me. Yet I thought it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother and fellow soldier, but your apostle, and the minister of my desire. Although he promised that he would send Timothy quickly, yet because there is still some delay when he said he would send him, he now sends Epaphroditus: it is necessary, he says, to send Epaphroditus to you. He commends the person; afterwards he added the reason. The commendation of the person is: a brother in the law, a fellow soldier in the camp and in the labour of the Gospel, but your apostle. See, he names Epaphroditus an apostle. For everyone who is sent, and who is sent for the sake of the Gospel, can be called an apostle. Indeed this is why those twelve, or eleven, were called apostles, from the ministry for which they were sent to preach. So whoever is sent for this can be called an apostle. And as for his saying your apostle: either because he is sent to you, for [he sends] others to other places; or [as] one whom you chose from among your own as apostle; yet, he says, the minister of my desire. And what is my desire? That you should hear, that you should hold fast the word.

Verse 26. — Because he was longing and yearning for you all. Now he adds the reason why he sends him: for he said he would send Timothy quickly, so that he might be of good heart, knowing how things stand with you. Now he sends this man, because he longs for you and yearns for you all, and it is grievous to him to be absent. And he proves that he takes it hard, thus: and he was distressed because you had heard that he was ill. He was labouring, he says, under this distress, and you had heard that he was ill in body, that is, sick. Or does he was distressed signify this: that he himself was the cause of his own being in sickness? and he was distressed from that very cause, and it came about because he longed and yearned for you? So from there I now send him to you.

Verse 27. — For indeed he was ill to the point of death: but the Lord had mercy on him; and not on him only, but also on me, so that I should not have sorrow. He shows why he either longed for the Philippians or was distressed: he was ill, he says, to the point of death. In such a sickness longings are great and vehement: he was sick, he says, to the point of death; but the Lord had mercy on him. See, since we experience a benefit from the Lord here in life too. Then, because we ought also to hasten to death? For although the world is the ministry of sin, and therefore to be fled, yet to desire life in the world is not a sin. And if it ought to be desired, it is rightly said, but the Lord had mercy on him. Then, since everything we do here for life, if we are also righteous, [profits] both ourselves at once and others, God deservedly has mercy on us and keeps us in life. So accordingly he adds: God had mercy not on him only, but also on me, so that I should not have sorrow. For if above [he was] called the minister of my desire, of Epaphroditus himself; for if I lost the minister of my desire, I would be grieved and have sorrow. Therefore many are preserved, and God has mercy on those through whom something is done that pertains to the ministry of salvation. At the same time we too ought to pray for such men, so that we may not have sorrow if we lose those whose help we use in carrying out, instilling and proclaiming divine things.

Verse 28. — I have therefore sent him the more hastily. He distinguished his sendings. For of Epaphroditus he says, I have sent. Of Timothy he says, I hope to send to you quickly. And yet above, I thought it necessary to send to you, is not about one whom he is going to send, but one already sent. Hence here he concluded, I have sent to you, so that when you see him you may rejoice again, and I may be without sorrow. He joined on this reason too for why he sent him. Above, for this reason: I have sent, because he longed for you and yearned for you; now, to the Philippians themselves: that you may be glad and rejoice again when you see him. What is rejoice again? That, since you were in sorrow, for so it was said above, you had heard that he was ill, you may now be glad again when you see him. Or again, because after his grave illness they heard that he had become well, and rejoiced, and now if they see him they will rejoice again? And as for his adding, and I may be without sorrow: because if he said above that Epaphroditus was the minister of his desire, then certainly, when he sends him away, he might seem as it were sorrowful; but since that man too longed for them, and they will rejoice if they see him, Paul will be able to be without sorrow.

Verses 29, 30. — Receive him therefore in the Lord with all rejoicing; and hold those who are of this kind in honour. Because for the work of Christ he came near to death, exposing his life to uncertainty, so that he might supply what was lacking to you in your service to me. This is a commendation, that they should receive Epaphroditus. And he gives grace and a reason to the commendation: in the Lord, he says, receive [him]; that is, [receive] him as one who is a minister of the Lord: you who are already in the Lord, love the minister of the Lord, and love [him] with all rejoicing. And he wants this shown generally to all who are such. Receive, he says, those who are of this kind. And what is receive him? Hold [him] in honour. He also gives reasons why he wants these things offered to such men: because for the work of Christ he came near to death. This is certainly about Epaphroditus; for while he wished, by labour of both mind and body, to do justice to the Gospel, that is, to preach the word of the Lord, he laboured much, and through a grave sickness came near to death. At the same time he shows both what befell Epaphroditus and what we ought to do. But how much did he labour? He came near to death, he says; and putting his life in uncertainty. Not uncertainty in what he was doing for you, but uncertainty in that he laboured to the point of danger, so that it was now uncertain whether he would live, because of the labour. And what did he do for you? So that he might supply what was lacking to you in your service to me: so that, since I was occupied, he might complete the service that was lacking towards me. For in truth, since the preaching is one and the teaching is one, only the labour can differ in the individual apostles and evangelists; yet what they teach is one. Accordingly, what did the apostle Epaphroditus himself fulfil? This service, he says, which was lacking to you, he completed.

Chapter 3. — Verses 1, 2, 3. — For the rest, brothers, rejoice in the Lord: to write the same things to you is for me not irksome, and for you it is plain. Be glad, he says, in the Lord, brothers, that it is not irksome to me to write the same things to you, while for you it is of the greatest profit. What I write is firm and safe. The Greek put it so as to say firm and safe; the Latin says plain. Beware of the dogs, watch out for the evil workers, look at the cutting-off. For we are the circumcision, who serve God through the Spirit, and exult in Christ Jesus, not trusting in the flesh. This admonition teaches not what is to be done, but what is to be avoided. And he warns them to keep themselves away from the Jews: beware, he says, of the dogs. There is a treatment of dogs: for divine Scripture also states that there are dogs which are useful and are defenders of the Church, as David teaches in Psalm 68, whom he says to be sated with the blood of enemies in the temple of God. And here he speaks against dogs, from whom he says one must beware; namely the Jews, who they are: that they are workers and evil. For workers spend their life in works, not knowing God, and hope for salvation for themselves from works; about whom it has already been said above that works avail nothing. Look, he says, at the cutting-off. As though among them there is a cutting-off, because they cut off a shameful part of the body. But we, he says, are the circumcision. For we circumcise all malice from our hearts: and we do this because we serve God through the Spirit, but they through the flesh; therefore they are cut off, not circumcised. Let us exult, he says; or rather, we exult. And where do we exult? Not in the flesh, as they do, having confidence, but in Christ Jesus. Therefore withdraw all your knowledge from the Jewish discipline, from the works of the Jews, from Jewish circumcision; and have circumcision of the heart, so that we may serve God through the Spirit and exult in Christ. But let them exult in the flesh, having confidence from it, that because they are circumcised in the flesh they can be saved and merit eternal life.

Verses 4, 5, 6, 7. — Although I too might have confidence even in the flesh. It is proved in many ways that the Jews have all their confidence in the flesh and in circumcision: since indeed the Jews even interpreted thus, that salvation came about when Moses was circumcised; from which it may be understood that the Jews place confidence concerning the flesh too, and more in the flesh. But Paul teaches this: if, he says, confidence is in the flesh, that is, in circumcision, I have more: for I, he says, have confidence in the flesh. Accordingly it is added thus: if anyone else thinks he trusts in the flesh, I more. And he teaches why, if anyone has confidence in the flesh, he himself has more. And so he shows his whole person to be Jewish in every way: in circumcision, birth, tribe, nation, law, administration under the law, and zeal of life too. And yet, though he had fulfilled all these things belonging to the Jewish discipline, all these, I say, he said were loss to him because of Christ, and because of the eminence of his flesh. All these things, then, will be proved in the statement thus. Circumcised on the eighth day: this is circumcision. By birth, he says, of the race of Israel. Likewise by tribe, Benjamin. Likewise by nation, a Hebrew of Hebrews. Likewise by law, as to the law a Pharisee. Likewise by zeal, as to zeal persecuting the Church. Likewise by life, as to the righteousness which is in the law, since I was without reproach. By all these, then, he proved that he had more confidence in the flesh and in circumcision; since he had all the things of the Jewish discipline, in blood, in nation, in mind, and in life. And as for his saying as to zeal persecuting the Church: [it means] that, having great zeal for the synagogue, he persecuted the church. Likewise his saying as to righteousness, that is, through conduct and life, by which a man is justified; yet he says in the law of the Jews. Since I was without reproach: so that I committed no crime, and did all that the law commanded. For that is righteousness among the Jews, from the law. But since righteousness now comes to us Christians from Christ, and we are justified because of him, Those things, he says, which were gain to me, I have counted as loss: that is, I understood that they caused me loss, holding all those things cheap because of Christ.

Verses 8, 9. — But he also added this: Because of the eminence of Christ Jesus our Lord. The Greek, however, has because of the eminence of the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ: so as to show that those things are both small and very little, and rather opposed, if they stand alone, for they are loss, he says; and this eminence of Christ is what excels and surpasses all things. For whose sake I have suffered the loss of all things, and I count them as dung. He concludes the sense: that he despises all those things, and suffers all losses for Christ, so that he may gain Christ. And what is I have suffered loss? All those things which had been glorious to me, both of blood, and of tribe, and of nation, and that I had been a Pharisee in the law, and that I had so kept righteousness as to be without reproach: all these cast aside, I have endured the loss of all things; and I have counted or count all those things as dung. For we read it better thus than I am counted; for the Greek too put it so, hēgoumai, not that he is counted by others, but that he counts all those former things as dung, and casts them away, and by a just judgement gains Christ. He himself adds: And may I be found in him. For this is to gain Christ: to be now in him, and to be joined to him by faith, and to perceive him, to have him.

Not having my own righteousness, which is from the law. That, namely, which I set out above, when I lived without reproach: for then it is as it were my righteousness, or ours, when we think that by our conduct we merit the righteousness of God, made perfect through conduct. But no, he says, not having this righteousness. But which? He adds that: But that which is from the faith of Christ, which he proclaimed; the righteousness from God, from faith. This righteousness, then, he says he has; not that which is from the law, which is in works, as I said, and in a fleshly discipline; but this which proceeds from God. What is that? Righteousness from faith, which is faith from the faith of Christ, that is, from us towards Christ. And he added most fully what the faith is that we have towards Christ, from which righteousness comes to us.

Verses 10, 11. — To know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings: sharing the burden of his death; if in any way I may come to meet [him] in the resurrection which is from the dead. He sets out the faith which we have in Christ, which he said he urges upon and proclaims to the Philippians, which proceeds from God, righteousness from faith, from the faith which he adds, to know him: what he is, who he is, whence he is. These things he then added about Christ, of course, and the power of his resurrection. Either in that he rose by power, for it is a great power to rise from the dead; or in that he rose for our salvation, for this is the power of his resurrection. And he proved the same by what follows: for, he says, if we have the fellowship of his sufferings, as he himself said, because we have been or are sharers of his death, therefore we shall also be sharers in him. This is the power of the resurrection, that we have the fellowship of his sufferings. And what is this fellowship? That we who believe in Christ endure sufferings, and all sufferings, even to the cross and to death: and from all these, out of knowledge and out of the fellowship of sufferings, resurrection comes about; and thence, when we are sharers of his death and burden, we are in some way made to meet [him], so that we may come to meet [him] in the resurrection, which is the resurrection from the dead. See what faith in Christ is; and he says he teaches this, teaching what must be done in life: namely that, as companions of Christ's suffering, we should both believe this and have this as our faith, that we shall come into the power of his resurrection, having been made, that is, sharers of the burden of his death, so that on this account we may in some way come to meet [him] in the resurrection which is from the dead. This is the reward, that the toil; that the life, this the merit and glory.

Verse 12. — Not that I have already received, or am already made perfect. He added this more forcefully, speaking indeed about himself; but it is for us to apply to ourselves what Paul says of himself. And what is this? That by those labours, and that endurance of fellowship in death and sufferings, we may be able to go to meet [him], and at the same time rise together in the resurrection of the dead. But not, he says, do I do these things because I have already received them or am already made perfect: for as long as anyone lives, he does not yet receive these things or is made perfect; for he is still engaged in the fellowship of his sufferings, since the fellowship of sufferings lasts until death. He does not yet receive, then, nor is he made perfect, but perseveres to the end of life, remaining in these same labours and in the true fellowship of his sufferings; then he will be able to go to meet [him] in his resurrection from the dead. Yet in this he also expressed doubt, by saying if in any way I may come to meet [him]. Because he is still alive, he therefore said if in any way. For when one perseveres in the fellowship of sufferings, and has become like [him] even in death itself, there is no doubt that he will come to meet [him] in the resurrection. And what is it to come to meet [him] in the resurrection of the dead? It is each person's life, made perfect and full and completed in every way from the fellowship of Christ's sufferings, at that time when the resurrection from the dead takes place, that is, when the dead are raised. That one, as Paul says speaking of himself, that one, I say, who has lived his life in full fellowship of his sufferings, comes to meet Christ: he is not [merely] raised, but comes to meet Christ. Others are only raised; but the perfect, and those who have suffered in every way as Christ did, will meet him, and will go to meet Christ as he comes; as he himself also said elsewhere. Rightly, then, he says if in any way, because he is still in life. And rightly he added, not that I have already received, or am already made perfect: but I pursue, that I may at some time lay hold, in that in which I was also laid hold of by Christ. You see that he says he is still in life, and that this is why he doubted above. For he still pursues Christ through all sufferings, so as to lay hold of Christ, that is, to come to Christ having been made a sharer in all his sufferings. For Christ by all his sufferings set free all who follow; and in a way he laid hold of all, but those who would follow. He who wishes to follow and lay hold of Christ must follow Christ in all sufferings, so as to lay hold of Christ in that in which he was also laid hold of by Christ. For if Christ set all free by his sufferings, he laid hold of all by his sufferings; in these, then, we are. That is, having been made a sharer with Christ through his sufferings, one lays hold of Christ in that in which one was laid hold of by Christ.

Verses 13, 14. — Brothers, I do not consider that I have laid hold. He still continues on what I said: that he is still alive, and therefore has not yet received, nor been made perfect, nor yet laid hold. For he said this: but I pursue, that I may in some way lay hold. So I consider that I have not yet laid hold, so that the Philippians may understand from this how far they are from the benefits of deliverance, when Paul himself, often engaged in so many sufferings of Christ, beaten, imprisoned, thrown to beasts, and loaded with other evils, yet does not consider that he has yet laid hold of Christ, since he is still alive and remains. Great is that participation in suffering through which we are truly joined, if we imitate Christ even in suffering. Yet one thing [I do]: consigning to oblivion the things that are behind, and stretching myself out towards the things that are ahead, according to the rule, I pursue towards the prize of the upward calling in Christ Jesus. Since, as we said, he spoke above thus, if in any way I may come to meet [him] in the resurrection of the dead, and we have shown why this doubt was expressed, because he is still alive, and many things could happen, and above all death itself, therefore he added that he does not consider he has yet laid hold of Christ. But he shows that he even now holds something in his purpose: one thing, he says. What is that? That all things which are past be consigned to oblivion, and he follow only the things that are to come, ahead; that is, in those things which are first before us, and are to be followed according to the rule and discipline of the precepts given by Christ, so that we may come to the prize of the upward calling, yet in Christ Jesus. There are, then, two precepts for the rest of life for one living in the Christian order, and who still lives by the rule: that all the things he has done, even if he does them well and rightly, he should not keep in his memory, as if by them he merited what he is to obtain; but should consign them to oblivion, and always thereafter pursue, as if new, the things that remain, yet living according to the rule, and always stretching himself out in it, and keeping the rule of a Christian up to the end in death, so that he may come to the prize.
