For to remember past things, even things rightly done, is first of all the mark of one who attributes and claims them for his own merit, when these things are not ours, and we do not obtain grace by our works. Secondly, somehow we become negligent about the things that are ahead, that is, the things that follow, through confidence that we do many things. Hence the apostle instructed that the things which are behind must all be consigned to oblivion. What we have said can also be taken [as referring to] the different life we have lived: as Paul himself, that he was a Jew, that he was a zealot of the law, and the rest: so that he called these things behind, and to be consigned to oblivion; as if each of us ought to consign his past life to oblivion. But the stronger sense is that we ought to consign to oblivion even a past life well conducted and lived rightly according to the rule, and stretch ourselves out towards the things that are ahead according to the rule, so that we may follow Christ to the prize of the upward, he says, calling. For from that time we are Christians, we have been called by God. This is the upward calling: for no one is called to God or by God except in Jesus Christ. For he himself is the door, he the propitiator, he the reconciler: and we have taught this in many places: and so life is and ought to be for us, that with Christ going before as leader, that is, by our faith in Christ, we may be able to come to the prize.

Verses 15, 16. — Let as many of us, then, as are perfect think this: and if you think otherwise in anything, this too God has revealed to you. From this it can be understood that we expounded truly what we said above, that we should consign to oblivion the things done by us under the right rule. For he joins on: as many, then, as are perfect, let them consign to oblivion all the things that have been done. For it is not by our merits but by the grace of God that we obtain the prize. Thus, then, he exhorts: let us think this, he says. Who should think this? As many of us as are perfect. And what should we think? That we should consign to oblivion the things that are behind; and indeed the present time too, that is, what we are now doing, is to be consigned to oblivion. Certainly if the present, then the past too, and the things we had in life: and that we should stretch ourselves out towards the things that are ahead according to the rule. Let us all, he says, think this, and all the perfect. As for what he adds, and if you think otherwise in anything, this too God has revealed to you: if the sense is complete and self-contained, not joined to what follows, it is to be understood thus: and if there is something about this very thing we have said which you take and understand otherwise, think so, I grant it to you; for he is speaking of the perfect, since he said thus, as many of us, then, as are perfect. So, you who are perfect, even if you think otherwise: and he concluded with a concession, this too God has revealed to you, it is good, since both this and that, what you think, and what I have said. But if it is not this, [namely] conceding, the sense will hang [on what follows], so that it is said thus: if you think otherwise in anything, and yet God has revealed this to you, he adds what is joined on: Yet let us think that which we have attained, that is, what we have taught, and to which we have been trained. For he adds thus: nevertheless, to that which we have attained, let us think that very thing, let us walk in the same. That is, from the time I proclaimed the Gospel to you, and to this point we have attained in our manner of living and understanding; that very thing, he says, let us think, and let us walk in the same; namely in that which we have attained: for by saying yet he as it were rejects [it]. What is above we do not admit, and the sense is this: that is indeed tolerable and to be done; but this above all. So even if you think otherwise, and even if God has revealed this to you, by which you think otherwise, nevertheless to that which we have attained, let us think that very thing. And what is that, to that which we have attained? What you once received from my admonitions, and what has now been instructed by me: for to this we have attained from all the admonition and precepts. And he says we have attained, namely by our precepts: that consigning to oblivion the things that are behind, we should stretch ourselves out towards the things that are ahead according to the rule, so that we may come to the prize of the upward calling in Jesus Christ. In this, then, he says, let us walk. So much does the earlier account concern that life and the precept for life. For it was said above, consigning to oblivion the things that are behind, let us stretch ourselves out towards the things that are ahead. For this is let us walk in it.

Verses 17, 18. — Be imitators of me, brothers. This is fitting to the thought we were speaking of: that they should do nothing new themselves, even if they think otherwise, even if they have something revealed by God. Be imitators of me, he says, brothers; so that what I do, what I instruct, what I practise in life, what I follow, this you too should imitate and follow. And observe those who walk in this way, as you have us as an example. He had given an instruction as to what perfect men should do, and afterwards he had added that they should not think otherwise, and had as it were made a concession; yet he concluded that they should rather follow him, and so walk as he himself did. Now, with a full exhortation, when he said, be imitators of me, he added an example, so as to persuade more easily: that it ought to be done for this reason, namely that others were doing it. Observe, he says, those who walk in this way, as you have us as an example. He concluded two things: those who walk as we do; and in that very point he briefly set out that he was an example to them, both one who was [an example] to others and one who ought to be [one] to these. That is, as those imitate me, so you too should have [me] as an example. For many walk, of whom I have often told you. He added more, so that they were not few who were seen to imitate him: many, he says, walk in this way. And he added another argument: lest I put before you an example today [only] for exhortation, there are many, he says, who walk as we do, of whom I have often spoken. So he did not bring forward for the occasion those who walked in this way, since he had already often spoken of them, that they walked in this way.

Verse 19. — But now I say it even with tears, [that they are] enemies of the cross of Christ; whose God is the belly, and glory in their shame, who think earthly things. The exhortation is greater when it comes from fear. For above it was from advantages and benefits. For there is an exhortation as to how they should live, towards the very thing he instructed above, since he himself urges and drives the Philippians to the same life, and he gave again another argument, that many already live in the same way, and many of whom Paul himself had often told the Philippians that they already lived so. This benefit of the exhortation is strengthened by a greater reason, what evil they will have to suffer if they live otherwise; and, as I said, persuasion from fear is greater. He added feeling too, being about to speak of the evils that those who live otherwise will suffer, by saying: I say it with tears. For I grieve and weep, because those who are enemies of the cross, that is, those who do not believe in this Gospel, namely that they should believe in Christ [as] man, that is, who was in man, who was born of Mary, was crucified. All heretics, then, who accept Christ neither as crucified nor as in man, who are many and various — these, I say, will have destruction as their end. For some said that he was a man, not that he was in man. Others deny altogether that he was born in the flesh, others deny that he was crucified. All these heretics, as I said, and those like them, will perish. For this is what he said, whose end is destruction: which indeed will follow men of this kind. And what they will suffer, and what they are, he enumerates thus: what they will suffer, whose end is destruction; what they are, whose God is the belly; what will follow, and glory, he says, in their shame. How they think, he added: who think earthly things. Concerning destruction: that their end is destruction, who do not believe these things, that is, who are enemies of the cross. For this is what he meant by being enemies of the cross of Christ: not believing the cross of Christ. These, I say, will perish, and their end is destruction.

But those who do not believe this, that is, who are enemies of the cross of Christ, how do they have the belly as God, of whom he said, whose God is the belly? There are in a way two [kinds], that is, one of two, who are enemies of the cross of Christ: for either, thinking carnally, they laugh at the cross of Christ, since they suppose that Christ [was] a man raised on the cross; not, in the mystery according to the Gospel, Christ crucified in man, by which he conquered sin and triumphed over the powers, and triumphed through the crucified flesh: this, I say, is the cross we hold in mystery. Others, as I said, accept the cross as [belonging to] a man, truly only a man: and for this reason they are enemies to the cross; and these, because they think carnally, despise the mystery of the cross: and these, as I said, think of the flesh, and judge nothing other than of the flesh, and for them God is the belly, and glory is in their shame, and these are those who think earthly things, whose end, however, is destruction. Or again, those who think Christ spiritual, and do not understand him [to have been] in the flesh, nor crucified; and for this reason they are enemies of the cross of Christ, and they too will have destruction as their end. And this part is concluded about them: although this part pertains also to those who think carnally of Christ; but the three things that follow pertain to those who think carnally of Christ: that their God is the belly, and glory in their shame, and they think earthly things.

Verse 20. — For our conduct is in the heavens. This is certainly the contrary of what precedes; yet [it answers] to that part where he said they think earthly things, judging that Christ is a man, and was a man, and was not in the flesh, but came with the flesh, as the Jews say he will come, and the other heretics. But we, on the contrary, have all our life and our conduct of living in the heavens, thinking that Christ came from heaven, put on flesh, was raised on the cross. Then he adds thus: whence also we await the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ. So that he both came from there and will come from there. For if he will come from there, he also came from there before. For he who ascended, he is also the one who descended. So we have our conduct in the heavens, because from there too we await the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will come to judgement in the last times; and he will be a Saviour to us, because we believe in him and await Christ.

Verse 21. — Who transfigured the body of our lowliness, that it may be of like form with the body of his glory, according to the working of his power, so that he may also subject all things to him. This passage too holds the mystery concerning the resurrection. For what Christ, placed in the flesh, accomplished in order to save souls, and so that immortality might be given also to the flesh through the resurrection, [this] the powers of his cross worked. And we await all these things, and our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who, he says, by that mystery by which he descended and was crucified and rose again, transfigured the lowliness or the figure of our body, or rather the body of our lowliness. How is this? Because when our lowly body rises and is changed, Jesus Christ transfigured the lowliness of our body for the better, or transfigured our lowly body into a magnificent one. That is, he gives it eternity, making a heavenly garment for it; so that it may be, he says, of like form with the body of his glory. For Christ is spirit, from which his body is form, and power; that very form which is power, the form of glory, is a divine and eternal body. But when we, rising, are changed, and have been made spiritual in soul and body and spirit — for thus these run together into one man, and they will be one spirit — then the body of our lowliness too [will be] of like form, that is, of the same and equal form with the body of the glory of Christ himself, so that we too may be spirit, as he too is spirit. And this will come about according to the working of his power. For every mystery and every action of Christ works this, completes this according to his power: that we come together into one, when soul and body and spirit will be [one], as he himself is spirit.

Again, because God is spirit, all things will be subjected to God when they are brought back to one power; and so, he says, he will be able to subject all things to him, namely to God. It may seem continuous and not connected in the sentence, since he put it thus, so that he may also subject all things to him, and did not set out beforehand to what we should refer to him. For if we refer to him to God, God has not been named above; it is obscure and not correct, and placed rather by the translator than by Paul. To what, then, do we refer to him? It is certain indeed that Christ works for this, to subject all things to God; but here there is no mention of God. To what, then, do we refer it? We must understand how briefly, and yet plainly, he set down God. For when he said that Christ, whom we await, transfigured the body of our lowliness, so that the very body of our lowliness may be of like form with the body of his glory, this is where the understanding of God is received, and God himself, when he said, according to the working of his power. For Christ did all things to take care of souls, to give eternity also to the flesh, and to make our body of like form with the body of his glory; but he did this according to the working of his power. For he worked, but [it was] his power through which he worked: and this is God; for he works through the Father. Christ indeed works: that is, the Father is in him, and works through him. So where he said of his power, there God is understood, to whom, that is, he subjects all things, and for this he works, so that he may also subject all things to him. And that he said also all things refers to the fact that he himself is subject to him. For the Word, which is Christ, is certainly subject to God, for God is more powerful. And this is proved by many things. He is the one who sends, this one the one who is sent; he the Father, this one the Son; this one he through whom the working is, he the worker. So if these things are so, Christ is to God in such a way that he himself is also subject. For thus it is said in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: but when all things have been subjected to him, then he himself will be subject to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all. Or is the sense that he said so that he may also, so that he not only makes the body of our lowliness of like form, but may also subject all things to him? For when all things that are either carnal or creatures have been overcome and changed, all things are rendered subject to the power of God, through which Christ works.

Chapter IV. — Verse 1. — Therefore, most beloved brothers, my joy and my crown, stand firm in the Lord. All virtue in Christians is charity and love, which cannot come about unless they have one essence and stand firm in one thing, thinking one thing; and this is what he now says: stand firm in the Lord, O most beloved brothers. From this it may be understood that he wants them to think one thing, when he says most beloved brothers. For it comes about that those who think one thing and stand firm in one thing love one another. In what one thing? In Christ, of course. For since all have faith in Christ equally, they stand firm in him. And if you, O Philippians, do this, you will be my joy and my crown. Verse 2. — I ask Euodia, and I ask Syntyche, to think the same thing in the Lord. So that these women too may think one thing in the Lord, that is, that believing in Christ, they may think and understand what the gospel holds concerning Christ. But I ask, he says, expressing that it will benefit them. For I do not command, I do not order, but I ask.

Verse 3. — So I beseech you too, true yokefellow, help those women who laboured together with me in the gospel, with Clement and my other helpers, whose names are in the book of life. We said above that Epaphroditus had promised to come to the Philippians; afterwards he shows that he has sent him, when he said, so I sent him the more hastily. So this is added as it were, so that he too may have his commission in the letter, and [Paul] asks and beseeches him to admonish those women, Euodia and Syntyche, to think the same thing in the Lord. Help, he says, those women who labour together with me in the gospel. How do they labour in the gospel? In that they too either recognise, guard and keep the very gospel that I proclaim, or themselves proclaim it, assert it, preach it; for women too, speaking in their own measure about the gospel, that is, about Christ and the whole mystery, preach the gospel.

Then he adds thus: with Clement and my other helpers, whose names, he says, are in the book of life. For so he records the mystery that all who have faith concerning Christ, and have faith in him, and speak of and instil that faith in Christ into people, are as it were helpers to the evangelists; and since this is so, their names are already in the book with God, because they will be in eternal life. And that this is Epaphroditus, to whom he gives this charge, to help the women mentioned above to think one thing, may be understood from the fact that he said, I beseech you too, true yokefellow; for indeed he spoke of him above thus: Yet I thought it necessary [to send] Epaphroditus, my brother, my fellow soldier. So there he said brother, here he said true; above he said fellow soldier, here he said yokefellow.

Verses 4, 5. — Rejoice; let your modesty be known to all people. This is what follows, that those who think one thing and have faith in one thing rejoice in the Lord and are always dear to one another. Rejoice, he says, in the Lord. That is too little; again I say, rejoice. For when you are joined in heart, you rejoice in the Lord; and when you rejoice in the Lord, you are joined in heart and stand firm in the Lord. Let your modesty, he says, be known to all people. For it bears greatly on the merit of the life to come and on the kingdom in the heavens if we live modestly. For modesty is the knowledge of each person that keeps to its measure and does not stretch and extend itself beyond itself. Indeed, when we, while we are here, recognise our lowliness (since we are among things not our own) and keep the measure of our lowliness, God will lift us up. So let your modesty, he says, be known to all people. Why does he urge this? That we may please here? No; but so that Christ, having recognised our lowliness, may raise [us] up and accept our modesty. For what does he add? The Lord is near. A great exhortation and a great precept, both from truth and from the force of persuasion. For since judgement is already at hand, and the end of this life is approaching for all, there ought to be haste in us to live with good conduct and great modesty; for the judgement and coming of the Lord are near.

Verse 6. — Bring nothing to anxiety. That is, do not take care for yourselves, and do not think about the world and worldly things or be anxious; for God provides all things necessary for you both now in this kind of life, and better things in that life which is eternal. But in every prayer and supplication, with good thanks, let your petitions be made known before God. So that every action of the faithful, good and perfect Christian, all anxieties being set aside (for this is renunciation), may be given to prayers and supplication. Prayers are asking the Lord; supplication is also speaking when you ask; for this is supplication, prayers with speech. But what will that supplication be? Asking something, or nothing? What is it that he asks for who, having now been made faithful, asks God? What supplication or petition, then, will he have, since he has renounced all worldly things? He himself urged that we should pray and supplicate with good thanks; so that for all of us supplication in prayers is thanksgiving, that we give thanks because we have obtained so great a gift by the goodness of God. For this is what he says, with good thanks. And he added good, so that we do not do it unwillingly, but truly give thanks, and then he added good thanks. Since supplication is in prayers, it can be about good thanks, it can be about petition. Above, when he had said with good thanks, he added: let your petitions, he says, be made known before God. But whose [petition] is not honourable? And let him ask that those heavenly things which are promised be fulfilled. He who asks, certainly asks for such things as it is right for one already faithful to ask. For when we think about what is to be asked, which we wish to be made known before God, they are necessarily such things as befit a faithful man who hopes for heavenly and all divine things. These, he says, that is, your petitions, let them be made known before God.

Verse 7. — And the peace of God, which holds all understanding, guard your hearts. This will be the reward if we pray thus, supplicate thus, that we supplicate with good thanks; and have our petitions such that they are made known before God. This being so, there will be, he says, the peace of God which guards your hearts; which peace of God holds all understanding. This is put forcefully and keenly; for when the peace of God has come into us, we will understand God: nothing dissonant, nothing discordant, nothing contentious through arguments, nothing that admits of question, as happens to us in worldly things; but all things are so open, when we have the peace of God, that all understanding is with us; for it belongs to peace to be at rest at last, to have security at last. When God entrusts peace to our hearts, all understanding is then with us. For he who understands God understands all things; when he understands God, the hearts of him who understands are guarded. Likewise your bodies in Jesus Christ. See, here too there is an indication of the resurrection; and this too is a reward set out or announced for those who ask thus and pray thus with good thanks, that they have the peace of God, and their bodies in Jesus Christ. For he spoke of the heart, of the understanding, that they will be guarded when peace is given; now of those very things, that is, of the body, of the soul: your bodies, he says, in Jesus Christ; for our bodies are in his majesty and power, which at his coming will rise, live again, receive their deserts; all of which will be whole for us if we keep those precepts, thinking one thing in Christ, rejoicing, modest, having no anxiety; in every prayer and supplication, with good thanks, making our petitions known before God.

Verses 8, 9. For the rest, brothers, whatever things are just, whatever holy, whatever lovable, whatever of good repute, if there is any virtue, if any praise, think on these things; what you have both learned and received, and also heard in me; do these things, and the God of peace will be with you. He has taught what sort of prayers we should have, that is, with good thanks, and likewise how [we should make] petitions; then what peace, that is, what benefit is given us by God; that we must act and ask thus, so that our understanding and our hearts may be guarded, and all our bodies may be in Christ Jesus. Since these things are so, for the rest, he says, brothers, think on these things. What is for the rest? After you have been corrected, all discord and error now removed, since you think one thing: for the rest, think thus: whatever things are true, accept and think on these. And what are those true things? Those set down in the gospel: Christ Jesus the Son of God, and the rest that we have often said. And when you think on true things, it follows that they are chaste; for what is true is not corrupted; for this is chaste: what is not corrupted is true. Then what is truly chaste is also just; for they are justified by sanctification from God. All things that are just, that are chaste, that are true, that are holy, are then also lovable, then also of good repute. For who would not love what is holy? Who would not speak and think well of it? So think, he says, on these things that pertain to good repute; certainly let them be lovable and have charity, and not have discord. For everything lovable has concord; likewise things of good repute have no envy and are in concord. Of all these, the former pertain to true virtue itself, the latter to the fruit of virtue. For it belongs to virtue to love what is true, chaste, just, holy; the fruit of virtue is what is lovable and of good repute. Therefore he set down these two things which he added: if there is any virtue, if any praise. He attends carefully to the force of things. For since all things come about by the grace of God — for he himself, through his Spirit sent into us, both governs and rules, so that nothing is [of] us — he therefore says, if there is any virtue. And again, if the virtue that is in us is not from us but from God, neither is the praise ours; and therefore, if any praise. Yet since it seems to be either our virtue or our praise, he therefore said there: think, he says, on all these things. What are they? What you have learned, with me teaching, of course, and received, and heard, and seen in me. He set down the completed thing first: you have learned. And from where have you learned? The causes are added: you have received. And again, from where [comes] the receiving itself? You have heard and seen: from me, you have seen in me; so that Paul is not only an admonisher but also offers an example of how true things are to be followed, how chaste things, how the rest. Do these things, he says. Above he said, think on these things; now he adds, do these things; so that these good things may be not only in thought but also in act. Then he added a reward as above: and the God of peace will be with you; a reward most necessary for the Philippians, that there be no discord, that all think one thing, that there be peace in their church; and the God of peace, who is the Father, and his Son Jesus our Lord, granting peace to every soul turned to God; this is what he says, peace be with you.

Verse 10. — But I rejoiced greatly in the Lord that at last you have flourished again, so that you also think on my behalf, as you were thinking before. Since the Philippians, though taught in the Gospel by the apostle Paul, had fallen into error, now, having been admonished, they have returned to their former understanding, so that they believe in the Gospel as it is announced. And you have flourished again, he says; that is, you have returned to flower: therefore I rejoiced in the Lord, and rejoiced greatly: and this is what he says, so that you think on my behalf: that is, so that you think as I taught you; for they had begun to think otherwise. And as to his saying, so that you think on my behalf: because your understanding and wisdom, which had been [at odds], was not on my behalf; but now, when you think as I taught and as I handed on the Gospel, you think on my behalf; that is, it can profit me, since I taught you. And what is that in which you were thinking before, [so that] now you have flourished again and, thinking the same, already think on my behalf?

Verse 11. — But you were occupied. I do not say this because of want. If this sense is joined to the preceding one, since it was said above, so that you also think on my behalf, that is, that you take thought for me, the meaning will be that you send the things I need; and indeed you have sent them; and so it may have been said, but I rejoiced in the Lord that at last you have flourished again, and fruit has begun to abound from your working. For so he says afterwards, and you began to think on my behalf: in which is also that phrase, in which you were thinking before, that you should send me what was necessary: and this is what follows. How were they thinking? Before, they were occupied, before, in these works. Which Paul indeed says: I do not say this, he says, because of want. For I do not say because of want that I wish you to think on my behalf, or in what you were thinking before, and in what you were occupied so as to send to me, or that I now wish you to send. For so he says afterwards too: not because I seek abundance in supplication. So I do not seek this because of need, but so that the fruit may be abundant in your supplication, when you care for all these things on my behalf and think [of them]: for that is what it is to take care; not because I am in need. For I also abound, he says; for I am sufficient to myself: for so he adds: For I have learned, in whatever circumstances I am, to be sufficient. The sense of I know is this: I know, he says, how to be sufficient in whatever circumstances I am: for I have learned to be content with what I have, and in whatever circumstances I am, to be sufficient to myself: for this is not to be referred only to expenses, but they ought to show care and thought and supplication on behalf of Paul: so that this is to be referred to everything: so that you also think on my behalf, in which you also thought. In general, then, [it means] that either necessities or supplication [and] care should be held by the Philippians on behalf of Paul. Finally, he set down this also not only with regard to fortunes or necessities of any kind:

Verse 12. — I know both how to be brought low and how to abound: and of the virtues [too], I know both how to be brought low and how to abound in all things, in the same way: that is, to display all the virtues. And in all things I have been trained. That is, accustomed to everything, both to bear thirst, hunger, cold, and again to rejoice in abundance. So both regarding virtues and regarding labours, in all things, he says, I have been trained; I have been trained both to be filled and to endure hunger, he says, both to be filled with plenty and again to endure hunger. Likewise he repeats the same two things: I can both abound and be in need in all things. By saying in all things, we have said that these things are to be referred not to the necessities of our living, but to everything that lies in action, labours and virtues. He said he had been so trained that he can both abound and be in need in all things. It is a new thing that he says I can be in need in all things: that is, I endure it when I am in need in all things, that is, when I am needy.

Verse 13. — And so that he may speak truly and nonetheless according to the Gospel teaching, he adds: Through him who strengthens me. This kind of life is always to be held and kept, so that we both labour and it is our practice to do all these things, fulfil them, bear them, endure them: yet in such a way that we believe this, that God has made us strong for all these things. For when he had said, I can be in need in all things, and endure hunger, he referred his strength back to God: through him who strengthens me. So also you, and all who have faith in God, should surely believe that whatever things there are, they can be made strong, both in need and in other labours. For God is never lacking to those who love him, who have faith and hope in him.

Verse 14. — Indeed you did well in sharing in my tribulation. That is, you were partakers or came to my help in tribulation, as sharing is, to be joined in like manner in a mystery: and he who suffers with another also comes to the help of the other.

Verse 15. — And you yourselves also know, Philippians, that in the beginning of the Gospel, when I set out from Macedonia, no church shared with me in the account of giving and receiving, except you alone. Here he has set out plainly what was said above, you shared in my tribulation, that is, you gave help and support by giving me necessities. Finally he adds this: you alone, he says, Philippians; and you also know that at the beginning of the Gospel, when I set out into Macedonia, I preached the Gospel through all the churches; but none, he says, shared with me. And where did it share? In the account, he says, of giving and receiving: that is, in expenses, which is given and received: for he who gives has an account with him who receives; and he who receives has an account with him who gives, of how much he gave and how much the receiver received. Not that the receiver himself also gave anything; but when one gives a gift, there is an account of giving and receiving. For what is there in which Paul could give money? But since there is an account of giving and receiving in money between those who give and those who receive, it was therefore phrased thus. For money is not received in return for the Gospel, so that the account of giving should be in money; it is far otherwise.

Verse 16. — You alone, he says, shared. Then he adds that they gave: Because even in Thessalonica you sent once and twice the things that were necessary for me. He has declared most plainly what it is that you shared and how there is an account of giving and receiving. You alone, he says, sent to Thessalonica once and twice the things that were necessary for me.

Verse 17. — Not that I seek the gift; but I seek fruit abounding in your supplication. I am not in need, he says, nor do I seek these necessities, but you ought only to have the practice of goodwill, so that I may have the fruit of your goodwill, in that you abound in goodwill; that is, so that when I make supplication concerning you, I may have the fruit of your goodwill. When I either ask God for you or give thanks to God for you, I have fruit in the supplication which is for you, as long as I understand that you abound and are well-disposed.

Verse 18. — For I have all things and abound. Therefore, he says, I do not seek the gift; for I have all things: and many have all things, but do not abound: for we can truly still want if we do not abound but [merely] have. He who abounds both has and has more than is necessary. For above he said, you sent what was necessary for me; now: These things, he says, I have and abound. Then he goes on to show the abundance: I am filled, having received what you sent through Epaphroditus. Lest what abounds should be someone else's, he says that it is also theirs, because they sent it: I am filled, he says, having received what you sent through Epaphroditus, an odour of sweetness, an acceptable sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God. If above he said he sought nothing else from what is given except abundant fruit, so here too, when he says he is filled and has received what was sent, [he means]: I do not rejoice and am not filled by what was sent, but by the fact that you had the will and the care to send; which is goodwill, and the fruit of abundance; whence it is an odour of sweetness to me that you are such; and a holy sacrifice, pleasing to God, is to do willingly what one does, to take care, to supply to another what must be supplied for his needs: this very thing, goodwill itself, is the sacrifice, both holy and acceptable and pleasing to God.

Verses 19, 20. — And may my God fulfil all your desire according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus. And to God and our Father be glory for ages of ages. Since he has said that [they are] upright in their very deeds, and good in their will, in that they send willingly and take care, and that this is the best sacrifice to God and an odour of sweetness, now, to return thanks, he wishes and makes a prayer that God (but let it be the apostle's God), my God, he says, so that it should not be shared with the rest, may fulfil all, he says, your desire, and fulfil it according to his riches. That is, since you will not have sought the things that are of the world, but those which God bestows and gives from his riches, that is, the things that are heavenly, the things that are divine; for these are the riches of God. Then he added, glory in Christ Jesus, so that these riches are those which are in Christ Jesus, that is, eternal life, sanctification. And he added what is always added with reverence, devotion and service: To God, he says, glory, to God the Father; and to God, he says, our [God], namely Jesus Christ, our Father: may there be to him eternal glory, which is for ages of ages.
The letter ends. Then, after the admonitions which [concern] living rightly, the greetings follow. First he greets [them] himself, or instructs [them] to greet others in his name. But which others?

Verses 21, 22. — Greet all the saints in Christ Jesus. The saints in Christ Jesus, or greet in Christ Jesus? The brothers who are with me greet you. Not only do I greet [you], he says, or bid you greet, but the brothers too greet you. He added who are with me. He wanted this to be understood of the people and of every Christian who is with him. Then another [greeting]: All the saints greet you, those whom, of course, he sanctified when they received faith: but especially those who are of Caesar's household: they especially greet you, those who are of the household of Caesar. And he shows the power of the gospel, in that many from Caesar's household have believed, who surely ought to have been haughty and to think of nothing but Caesar; and again [he shows] their humility, in that they are both humble and hospitable, and greet all the brothers placed elsewhere. As for his saying especially, it may be understood that they take pains to please in service, and for that reason he said, apart from the rest, that they send greetings.

Verse 23. — The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. He thought of the Philippians in such a way that he did not take them, as in the other letters, [as needing] to think rightly, nor [as] led astray by false apostles, but [the letter] was written only as an exhortation and in prayer. The grace, he says, of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. For if the Spirit is within, they think rightly. What then do the apostle's prayers do? [They ask] that the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with their spirit in Christ Jesus. Amen.
Here ends Victorinus's commentary on the letter of Paul the apostle to the Philippians.
